If you use heirlooms for whatever reason, as long as it's not "heirlooms taste better", then that isn't relevant here. But I see some people saying heirlooms are "just better", which is pretty much just plain wrong if you're thinking about it as a food.

The problem is people associate grocery store quality tomatoes with hybrids and think that it's the breed that causes them to taste like shit. That's not even remotely true, a lot of the same varieties they grow are grown by people at home who will happily say they're objectively better than anything they got in the grocery store, or have ever grown before.

The main advantage hybrids have is most of them are bred for higher yield, and produce far more on average than an heirloom. So in addition to disease/weather resistance or whatever, you get a bigger yield per square foot of area taken up.

Nothing wrong with heirlooms at all, they're cool and it's great to save seeds. But I just don't want people coming in thinking they did something wrong by buying hybrid seeds from a big catalog company.

I think there is the idea that hybrids is the same things as gene-splicing genetic engineering, which isn't necessarily true. But heirlooms are important for preserving genetic variety which has been wiped out by industrial-scale farming and GMOs.

All Earth creatures are genetic mutations. Some end up more burdened than others, some more robust. It's a common misconception that evolution always optimizes everything. Instead, it's always just going for 'good enough' and only optimizes until that point is reached, then stops.

Humans as a species have specialized on technology to help them out. Kind of like bees, ants, and hermit crabs. We're doing fine, our evolutionary pressure is minimal, and our greater worry is that we might be doing 'too fine' even than is sustainable.

For animals, Darwinism still happens. We just don’t see it because the time frame is too short.

As for humans, some countries are going backwards. America is one. A good living standard allows faulty genes to persist.

As I've just explained: "Darwinism" merely goes for the 'good enough' -- that is: good enough to avert evolutionary pressure. From an evolutionary POV, there's no "faulty genes" as long as that threshold is passed. So for instance, you may feel that red-hairedness is a "faulty gene" because you feel it's ugly, but nature doesn't give a fuck. However, if you were to create a regime that seeks to exterminate red-haired people, this might create an evolutionary pressure that could lead to the removal of those genes from the gene pool.
